concepts.name: Mechanism of Monsoon Origin: ITCZ vs. Jet Stream Theory
key_dimensions: Traditional thermal low theory vs. modern dynamic meteorology explanation
Role of Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) shifting northward over the Gangetic plain
Subtropical Jet Stream's role in onset — disappearance over Tibet as a trigger
UPSC trap: distinguishing between 'cause' and 'precondition' for monsoon onset

concepts.name: Role of Tibetan Plateau as a Heat Engine in Monsoon Onset
key_dimensions: Tibetan Plateau acting as an elevated heat source above 4,500m — sensible heat flux mechanism
Formation of the Tibetan anticyclone at upper troposphere and its linkage to South Asian monsoon
Why monsoon onset is later without Tibetan heating — comparison with ocean-only models
UPSC trap: Tibetan Plateau role is often confused with Himalayan barrier role (two distinct functions)

concepts.name: Southwest Monsoon: Normal Onset Dates and Progression Pattern
key_dimensions: Official onset over Kerala — IMD's declared normal date (June 1) and criteria for declaration
Progression timeline: Kerala → Arabian Sea branch vs. Bay of Bengal branch bifurcation
Bay of Bengal branch reaching northeast India before northwest India — why it moves faster
UPSC trap: the monsoon does NOT advance uniformly west to east — the northeast gets it earlier than northwest

concepts.name: IMD Criteria for Declaring Monsoon Onset over Kerala
key_dimensions: Five specific criteria: rainfall over 14 of 14 stations, OLR threshold, wind speed and direction at 925 hPa
2017 revised criteria replacing the older single-station Thiruvananthapuram rainfall benchmark
Distinction between 'pre-monsoon showers' (Mango/Kaal Baisakhi) and actual onset
UPSC trap: Onset declaration is probabilistic and criteria-based, not simply 'first rain in Kerala'

concepts.name: Arabian Sea Branch vs. Bay of Bengal Branch: Comparative Dynamics
key_dimensions: Arabian Sea branch: stronger in moisture content, hits Western Ghats first, causes orographic rainfall
Bay of Bengal branch: deflected by Arakan Mountains, enters through northeast India and Ganga plains
Why the Arabian Sea branch contributes more to total Indian rainfall despite Bay of Bengal branch arriving first in northeast
UPSC trap: the Arabian Sea branch is more moisture-laden but the Bay of Bengal branch covers more of the subcontinent

concepts.name: Monsoon Onset over Kerala: Early vs. Late Onset and Its Implications
key_dimensions: Historical range of onset dates (May 11 earliest to June 18 latest)
El Niño years associated with delayed onset; La Niña years with early onset
Cascading effect of delayed onset on kharif crop calendar and reservoir levels
UPSC trap: early onset over Kerala does NOT guarantee early or above-normal rainfall across India

concepts.name: Somali Jet (Low-Level Jet Stream) and Its Role in Monsoon Intensity
key_dimensions: Cross-equatorial flow along the East African coast as the source of Arabian Sea moisture
Somali Jet intensification linked to above-normal southwest monsoon years
Connection between Mascarene High (south Indian Ocean anticyclone) and Somali Jet strength
UPSC trap: Somali Jet is a LOW-level phenomenon (850 hPa), unlike subtropical jet which is upper-level

concepts.name: Break Monsoon: Definition, Causes, and Regional Impact
key_dimensions: Synoptic conditions: monsoon trough shifts from its normal position to the foothills of Himalayas
During break: rainfall increases over Himalayan foothills and northeast; decreases over peninsular India
Distinction between 'break monsoon' and 'withdrawal of monsoon' — temporal and spatial difference
UPSC trap: during a break, rainfall doesn't stop everywhere — it intensifies in specific regions

concepts.name: Monsoon Trough (ITCZ Over India): Position and Its Rainfall Implications
key_dimensions: Normal position of the monsoon trough connecting low-pressure areas from Rajasthan to Bay of Bengal
Northward shift = break monsoon; southward shift = active monsoon over peninsular India
Role of low-pressure systems and cyclones forming in the Bay of Bengal moving along the trough
UPSC trap: the monsoon trough is NOT a stationary feature — its daily oscillation determines regional rainfall distribution

concepts.name: Normal Withdrawal of Southwest Monsoon: Dates, Direction, and Criteria
key_dimensions: Withdrawal begins from northwest Rajasthan around September 17 (revised IMD normal)
Withdrawal is the REVERSE of onset — moves from northwest to southeast (last withdrawal from Tamil Nadu coast by December)
IMD criteria for withdrawal: no rainfall for 5 days, anti-cyclonic circulation established at 850 hPa, low humidity
UPSC trap: withdrawal begins from the NORTHWEST (opposite of onset from southwest) — a classic exam confusion point

concepts.name: 2020 IMD Revision of Normal Monsoon Dates (Updated Climatological Normals)
key_dimensions: IMD updated the base period from 1961–1990 to 1981–2010 for calculating normal dates
Onset over Kerala revised from June 1 to June 1 (unchanged), but withdrawal dates revised significantly
Withdrawal from northwest India advanced by about a week compared to earlier normals
UPSC trap: 'normal' dates are statistical averages revised periodically — not fixed astronomical dates

concepts.name: Northeast (Retreating) Monsoon: Onset, Coverage, and Contribution
key_dimensions: Occurs October–December as southwest monsoon withdraws and winds reverse over Bay of Bengal
Primarily benefits Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, and Sri Lanka
Why Tamil Nadu receives most rainfall during retreating monsoon (windward side during NE monsoon)
UPSC trap: Northeast monsoon is NOT just the 'withdrawal' of SW monsoon — it is a distinct seasonal wind system bringing its own rainfall

concepts.name: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Indian Monsoon Variability
key_dimensions: El Niño (warm ENSO phase): weakens Walker circulation, reduces moisture flux, associated with deficient monsoon
La Niña: strengthens monsoon; exceptions exist (1997 El Niño didn't cause drought — Indian Ocean Dipole offset)
Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) as a modulating factor that can counteract El Niño's negative impact
UPSC trap: El Niño does NOT always cause drought in India — relationship is probabilistic, not deterministic

concepts.name: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Its Independent Influence on Monsoon
key_dimensions: Positive IOD: warmer western Indian Ocean, cooler eastern — enhances moisture supply to India
2019 example: strong positive IOD offset El Niño, leading to above-normal monsoon despite El Niño conditions
Negative IOD: opposite effect, can amplify El Niño's drought-inducing tendency
UPSC trap: IOD is an INDIAN OCEAN phenomenon, unlike ENSO which is Pacific Ocean — both independently affect monsoon

concepts.name: Orographic Effect of Western Ghats on Southwest Monsoon Rainfall Distribution
key_dimensions: Windward (western) slopes: heavy rainfall (Cherrapunji-equivalent on west coast like Agumbe, Mahabaleshwar)
Rain shadow effect on Deccan Plateau — Pune, Solapur receive significantly less rainfall
Why Mumbai receives heavy rainfall but Pune (~150 km inland) receives only ~700mm
UPSC trap: Western Ghats create a rain shadow for the ARABIAN SEA branch; the Bay of Bengal branch creates its own orographic effects on eastern ghats (much weaker)

concepts.name: Pre-Monsoon Phenomena: Kal Baisakhi, Mango Showers, Blossom Showers
key_dimensions: Kal Baisakhi (Nor'westers): convectional thunderstorms in West Bengal and northeast during April–May
Mango showers: pre-monsoon convective rains in Kerala and Karnataka benefiting mango and coffee crops
Blossom showers (Kerala) and Cherry Blossoms (Karnataka coffee regions) — same phenomenon, different names
UPSC trap: these are PRE-monsoon local phenomena driven by local convection, NOT part of the southwest monsoon system

concepts.name: Active and Weak Monsoon Spells: Synoptic Systems Driving Variability
key_dimensions: Low-pressure systems and depressions forming in Bay of Bengal as primary drivers of active monsoon spells
Frequency of Bay of Bengal cyclogenesis correlating with intra-seasonal monsoon variability (Madden-Julian Oscillation link)
Western disturbances during monsoon season — role in triggering rainfall events in northwest India
UPSC trap: most of India's kharif rainfall depends on episodic low-pressure systems, NOT continuous steady monsoon flow

concepts.name: Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and Its Intra-Seasonal Monsoon Variability
key_dimensions: MJO: an eastward-moving 30–60 day atmospheric wave that modulates global tropical rainfall including India
Active MJO phase over Indian Ocean = enhanced monsoon; suppressed phase = break-like conditions
MJO's role in predicting monsoon onset timing over Kerala at seasonal scale
UPSC trap: MJO is an INTRA-SEASONAL variability driver (30–60 days), distinct from ENSO which is inter-annual — both affect monsoon at different time scales

concepts.name: Monsoon Onset over Northeast India: Why It Precedes Onset over Rest of India
key_dimensions: Bay of Bengal branch deflected by Arakan Yoma mountains enters Assam and Northeast before heading westward
Northeast India onset typically around late May to early June — before the official Kerala onset date
Funnel effect of Bay of Bengal narrowing at the north, concentrating moisture flux toward northeast
UPSC trap: Northeast India receives monsoon BEFORE Kerala in terms of actual rainfall, but Kerala is the 'official' onset point — a classic factual trap

concepts.name: Long Period Average (LPA) Rainfall and Classification of Monsoon Years
key_dimensions: IMD defines LPA (1971–2020 base period) as ~87 cm for June–September all-India average
Classification: Normal (96–104% of LPA), Excess (>110%), Deficient (<90%), Drought (<75%)
Why spatial distribution matters more than all-India average — a 'normal' year can have drought in some regions
UPSC trap: 'below normal' and 'deficient' are NOT the same category — IMD has precise percentage thresholds for each classification
